opus-5.5.text:
Yes, this is something I've been thinking about a lot. Classical statistics treats hypothesis testing as a single-agent problem: there's a statistician, there's some data, you pick a threshold, you control your type I error at 5% or whatever. That's the whole story in the textbook.

But that's not what happens in the real world. In drug regulation you have at least two agents with very different incentives. There's the regulator, say the FDA, who wants to approve good drugs and keep bad ones off the market. And there are the pharmaceutical companies, who know a lot more about their candidate drugs than the regulator does. They have private information, and they decide which drugs to put into trials at all. A phase III trial costs maybe tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, but a successful drug can earn billions.

So think about the economics. If the payoff from approval is huge relative to the cost of a trial, then even a drug the company privately believes is probably ineffective is worth testing. If you run enough of those, some will clear the 0.05 threshold by chance. So the regulator's nominal type I error control on each trial doesn't translate into control over the fraction of bad drugs that reach the market. The statistical guarantee is undermined by the incentive structure. It's a multiple testing problem, but the multiplicity is created strategically by another agent you don't control.

What we've argued, in work with Stephen Bates and colleagues, is that you need to design the statistical protocol and the incentives jointly. It's a contract theory problem, a principal-agent problem, with statistics inside it. You can ask what threshold, or more generally what menu of contracts, makes it rational only for companies with genuinely promising drugs to go to trial. The answer depends on the cost of the trial and the profit from approval. If profits are very large, a fixed p-value threshold may simply be too lenient, and the regulator would need stricter evidence standards, or a mechanism where the company puts something at stake.

A concrete way to think about this is e-values, which have a natural betting interpretation. The company effectively places a bet on its drug, and it only gets a big payoff if the evidence comes in strongly. That lines up incentives with honest reporting of the private belief. Good companies are happy to make that bet, and companies pushing marginal drugs find it's not worth it.

The broader point, and this is what I keep pushing on, is that machine learning and statistics have mostly been framed around a single decision-maker optimizing something. But a lot of the important problems are about collectives, markets, many agents with asymmetric information. Once you take that seriously, the statistical guarantees you thought you had can evaporate, and you need economics, mechanism design and incentive theory, sitting right alongside the inference. Drug regulation is just a very clean example where the stakes are high and the economics is completely transparent.

r001.rationale: The response describes strategic trial selection and multiple testing, but does not identify this as a departure from the classical i.i.d. data assumption.

r002.rationale: It mentions companies’ private information, but does not say regulators can probe hidden motivations or that those motivations are not arbitrary.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss offering service and price options to accommodate customers’ privately known needs.

r004.rationale: It proposes incentives that could make only promising drugs worth testing, but does not state that this enables system-wide control of statistical errors.

r005.rationale: It says that when approval profits greatly exceed trial costs, testing a drug believed probably ineffective can still be worthwhile, and chance may then clear the approval threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually a very deep question, and it's one where I think the statistical community has been a little bit naive historically. We've tended to think about error control as a purely mathematical problem. You have a false discovery rate, you have a family-wise error rate, you set your alpha, you do your multiple testing correction, and you're done. And that's fine if there's one scientist in a room running a fixed set of experiments.

But drug regulation isn't that. It's a multi-agent system. You have pharmaceutical companies who are strategic actors. They have enormous financial stakes, they choose which trials to run, which endpoints to pre-register, which results to submit, and when to stop. The regulator is sitting on the other side trying to make inferences from data that was generated by someone with an incentive. And once you have that, the classical error guarantees really don't hold in the way the textbook says they do. The p-value you're looking at is conditional on a selection process you can't see.

So what I've been arguing is that you have to bring economics and statistics together. You have to think about this as a mechanism design problem. What's the protocol such that, even when the submitting party is behaving in their own self-interest, the regulator still ends up with valid error control? There's some lovely recent work on this. People have started thinking about things like the regulator holding a budget of error, almost like an alpha-wealth, that gets spent down and replenished as a company submits hypotheses over time. And the nice thing is that it turns the incentive around. If the company knows that submitting junk depletes their future ability to get things approved, they self-select toward the drugs they actually believe in. The error control emerges from the incentive structure rather than being imposed by fiat.

And I think this is a general lesson, not just about drugs. We've built a field, machine learning included, that produces predictions and decisions, but we've mostly ignored the fact that those decisions sit inside markets where people respond. The moment you deploy a statistical procedure into a world of strategic agents, the procedure becomes part of the game. If you don't model that, your guarantees are fictional. So to me, the interesting frontier is not better test statistics, it's thinking about information, incentives, and uncertainty as a single design problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes strategic trial and result selection that undermines classical error guarantees, but does not identify this as a departure from the iid data assumption.

r002.rationale: It says companies are strategic actors and regulators cannot see the selection process, but does not say regulators can probe hidden motivations because those motivations are not arbitrary.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss offering different service or price options to accommodate privately known customer needs.

r004.rationale: It proposes that companies face future costs when submitting junk, encouraging them to self-select drugs they believe in, so error control emerges from the incentive structure.

r005.rationale: It mentions companies’ financial stakes, but does not explain that profit from an erroneous approval could incentivize submission of ineffective drugs.

astra-6.text:
Well, statistical errors don’t arise in a vacuum. There are people making decisions about which experiments to run, which results to report, and which drugs to bring forward. Those people respond to incentives. If the reward is for getting a drug approved, and approval depends on crossing a statistical threshold, you create an incentive to find ways to cross that threshold. That’s different from creating an incentive to produce reliable evidence of a clinical benefit.

A regulator can control a false-positive rate for a well-defined experiment. But if there’s a whole process of selecting experiments and selecting results, the guarantee for that one experiment doesn’t necessarily describe the error rate of the overall process. You have to look at the system that generated the evidence.

So I would view this partly as a mechanism-design problem. How do you make it worthwhile to disclose negative results, to replicate findings, and to keep learning after approval? Statistical methodology is essential, but it has to sit inside an institutional structure where producing good evidence is in the participants’ interest. Otherwise, you’re asking a statistical test to solve an economic problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes selection of experiments and results as a concern, but does not identify this as a departure from the classical i.i.d. data assumption.

r002.rationale: It says decision-makers respond to incentives, but does not state that regulators can probe hidden motivations or that those motivations are not arbitrary.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss offering different service and price options to accommodate customers’ privately known needs.

r004.rationale: It advocates making good evidence worthwhile and discusses system-wide errors, but does not propose incentivizing companies to submit drugs they have reason to believe are effective.

r005.rationale: It notes that rewards for approval can encourage efforts to cross a statistical threshold, but does not explain that profit from erroneous approval can motivate submission of ineffective drugs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at the whole system of incentives. A statistical guarantee applies to a particular procedure under particular assumptions. But if a company can try many compounds, many endpoints, many analyses, and then bring forward the one that looks good, the regulator is seeing a selected result. The nominal error rate for that one test doesn’t necessarily describe the error rate of the whole process.

And that doesn’t require anyone to be dishonest. If the reward is for getting a drug approved, people will naturally search for ways to satisfy the approval criterion. So the question becomes: can we design the process so that the economically attractive behavior also produces reliable evidence? Preregistering trials, making negative results visible, and requiring independent confirmation can help. But each of those has costs, and those costs affect which drugs get developed at all.

So I would view this as a problem involving statistics and economics together. You need to understand what evidence a test provides, but also why that particular test, on that particular drug, is the one that arrived at the regulator’s desk.

r001.rationale: The response describes how searching across compounds, endpoints, and analyses creates a selected result, but it does not identify this as a departure from the classical i.i.d. data assumption.

r002.rationale: It does not say regulators can probe companies’ hidden motivations or that those motivations are not arbitrary.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss offering service or price options to meet customers’ privately known needs.

r004.rationale: It suggests aligning economic incentives with reliable evidence, but does not propose incentivizing companies to submit drugs they have reason to believe are effective as a means of system-wide statistical error control.

r005.rationale: It mentions rewards for approval encouraging efforts to satisfy approval criteria, but does not state that expected profit from an erroneous approval can motivate submission of ineffective drugs.
